name: Lumen Wrasse
summary: An original, stylised wrasse created for Reef Ascension: a curious generalist that starts as a fingernail-sized juvenile and can grow into a formidable reef hunter.
fact: Real wrasses are among the most diverse reef fish families, ranging from tiny cleaners to the enormous humphead wrasse.
stylization: Fictional species. Real fish do not grow from juvenile to adult in minutes — continuous growth is a game mechanic.

name: Silver Sprat
summary: A slender silvery round herring that lives in shimmering schools over lagoons and reef flats, filtering tiny zooplankton.
fact: Schools of sprats are a vital food source for almost every reef predator, linking plankton to the rest of the food web.

name: Neon Damsel
summary: An electric-blue damselfish that hovers over rubble and coral, darting down to shelter when danger appears.
fact: Damselfish often defend small patches of reef and will chase away fish many times their size.

name: Black & White Spinecheek
summary: A timid monocle-bream-like reef dweller that hovers near sand patches, picking worms and tiny crustaceans from the bottom.
fact: Spinecheeks are named for a small backward-pointing spine beneath the eye.

name: Achilles Tang
summary: A dark surgeonfish with a blazing orange teardrop around the scalpel spine at its tail. Grazes algae in the surge zone.
fact: Surgeonfish carry scalpel-sharp spines at the base of the tail, which they can flick at attackers.

name: Palette Surgeonfish
summary: Royal blue with a black "painter's palette" marking and a yellow tail. Feeds on plankton above branching coral.
fact: When threatened, palette surgeonfish wedge themselves deep into coral branches and play dead.

name: Whitemargin Unicornfish
summary: A grey surgeonfish relative whose forehead grows a long horn with age. Grazes algae and gulps plankton along the reef wall.
fact: Unicornfish develop their horn-like snout as they mature; juveniles have none.

name: Pygmy Parrotfish
summary: A small parrotfish with fused, beak-like teeth that scrape algae from dead coral and nibble seagrass.
fact: Parrotfish grind coral rock while feeding and excrete it as fine sand — they help build white sand beaches.

name: Threadfin Butterflyfish
summary: A delicate deep-bodied butterflyfish with a trailing dorsal thread, nipping coral polyps, anemone tentacles and worms.
fact: A dark bar hides the real eye while a spot near the tail acts as a false eye, confusing predators about which way it will flee.

name: Long-nosed Butterflyfish
summary: A yellow precision nibbler whose forceps-like snout plucks tiny crustaceans, tube feet and tentacles from crevices.
fact: Its long snout lets it feed on parts of animals (like urchin tube feet) without being impaled.

name: Longfin Spadefish
summary: A tall, disc-shaped generalist with very long fins that eats algae, soft invertebrates and the occasional small fish.
fact: Juvenile spadefish (batfish) drift on their sides, mimicking dead leaves to avoid predators.

name: Moorish Idol
summary: An iconic banded fish with a flowing dorsal streamer, browsing sponges and algae from the reef.
fact: Moorish idols are one of the few fishes that feed heavily on chemically defended sponges.

name: Semicircle Angelfish
summary: A regal sponge specialist. Juveniles wear bright semicircular rings that fade into speckles as they mature.
fact: Angelfish can digest sponges that are full of glass-like spicules and noxious chemicals other fish avoid.

name: Redtoothed Triggerfish
summary: A purple-blue triggerfish that gathers in loose groups on current-swept slopes, snapping at plankton and sponge.
fact: Triggerfish can lock their first dorsal spine upright with a second spine — the "trigger" — wedging themselves into holes.
stylization: Its "repeat bite" behaviour on renewable food follows the reference game; Balanced rules limit point farming.

name: Clown Triggerfish
summary: A boldly spotted triggerfish whose powerful beak crunches crabs, urchins and shellfish.
fact: Triggerfish often flip urchins over to attack the less spiny underside.

name: Blackspotted Puffer
summary: A slow, round puffer that nips coral tips and crunches crustaceans with its beak. It inflates when threatened.
fact: Pufferfish tissues contain tetrodotoxin, making them extremely poisonous to most would-be predators.

name: Longhorn Cowfish
summary: A slow boxfish encased in a rigid bony carapace with two long horns. Blows jets of water to uncover prey in sand.
fact: Boxfish and cowfish can release a toxin from their skin when stressed.

name: Lionfish
summary: A slow, flamboyant predator armed with venomous spines. Herds small fish with fan-like pectoral fins, then gulps them.
fact: Lionfish venom is delivered by spines on the back, pelvic and anal fins — its flesh is not poisonous.

name: Devil Scorpionfish
summary: A lumpy master of disguise that lies motionless on rubble, then engulfs passing fish in a split second.
fact: When disturbed it flashes bright orange and yellow patterns hidden on the inner pectoral fins.

name: Painted Frogfish
summary: A pudgy ambush predator that walks on its fins and dangles a lure on its head to attract fish.
fact: Frogfish can swallow prey nearly as large as themselves with one of the fastest strikes of any fish.

name: Cleaner Mimic Blenny
summary: A blenny that copies the colours and dance of the bluestreak cleaner wrasse — then bites chunks of fin from trusting clients.
fact: False cleanerfish have fang-like teeth; experienced reef fish learn to avoid them.
stylization: Bites on much larger fish are a stylised nibble that damages but rarely kills the target.

name: Flashlightfish
summary: A dark nocturnal fish with glowing light organs beneath its eyes, used to find plankton and signal to its school.
fact: Its light comes from symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria; it "blinks" by covering or rotating the organs.

name: Lined Cardinalfish
summary: A big-eyed striped cardinalfish that hides among branching coral by day and schools out to feed at night.
fact: In many cardinalfish species the male broods the eggs in his mouth until they hatch.

name: Bluegill Longfin
summary: A secretive longfin that lurks in crevices by day and hunts small fish and shrimp under cover of darkness.
fact: Longfins have a blue-edged gill cover that may startle or warn rivals.

name: Bronze Sweeper
summary: A coppery schooling fish that packs into caves by day and spreads out to feed on plankton at night.
fact: Dense sweeper schools turn and flash in unison, confusing predators.

name: Bloodspot Squirrelfish
summary: A red, big-eyed fish that shelters in crevices and hunts crabs and shrimp mostly after dark.
fact: Red light fades quickly underwater, so red fish like squirrelfish look dark and inconspicuous at depth and at night.

name: Whitespot Hawkfish
summary: A perch-and-pounce hunter that sits on top of coral heads, watching for small fish and shrimp below.
fact: Hawkfish perch on thickened lower pectoral fin rays, as if standing on the coral.

name: Yellowspot Emperor
summary: An opportunistic emperor that cruises sand and seagrass edges for fish, crustaceans and mollusks.
fact: Emperors (family Lethrinidae) are important predators that switch prey depending on what is abundant.

name: Oriental Sweetlips
summary: A thick-lipped, black-striped benthic hunter that rests under ledges by day and sucks invertebrates from the bottom.
fact: Juvenile sweetlips swim with an exaggerated wriggle that may mimic toxic flatworms.

name: Dash-and-Dot Goatfish
summary: A sand-sifter with sensitive chin whiskers (barbels) that probe the bottom for buried worms and crustaceans.
fact: Wrasses and other fish often follow foraging goatfish to snatch prey they flush from the sand.

name: Clown Coris
summary: A wrasse with a shell-crushing bite that flips rubble to reach snails, clams, crabs and urchins.
fact: Juvenile clown coris wear two large false eyespots on the dorsal fin, which fade as they grow.

name: Ringtail Wrasse
summary: A pale-ringed carnivorous wrasse that patrols coral slopes for small fish, crabs and brittle stars.
fact: Many wrasses sleep buried in sand or wrapped in a mucus bubble at night.

name: Humphead Wrasse
summary: A massive, lumbering wrasse with thick lips and a bulging forehead, cracking hard-shelled prey with powerful jaws.
fact: Humphead wrasses are among the few predators of crown-of-thorns starfish and even eat toxic boxfish.

name: Rainbow Runner
summary: A torpedo-shaped jack with electric blue and yellow stripes, built for long, fast pursuits in open water.
fact: Rainbow runners sometimes rub against sharks, possibly to remove parasites.

name: Crocodile Needlefish
summary: A long, silvery surface hunter with needle-like jaws that strikes in straight-line bursts.
fact: Needlefish can leap clear of the water when startled, and their sharp beaks have injured boaters.

name: Small Spotted Pompano
summary: A silvery jack with a row of small dark spots along its flank, cruising reef edges at high speed.
fact: Pompanos have deeply forked tails built for sustained fast swimming.

name: Blackfin Barracuda
summary: A long, fang-toothed hunter that hangs motionless in the current, then explodes into a lightning-fast chase.
fact: Blackfin barracuda often form slowly circling schools by day that disperse to hunt at night.

name: Doublelined Mackerel
summary: A schooling reef mackerel with two lateral lines, sweeping in from open water to ambush baitfish.
fact: Mackerels must keep swimming to push water over their gills.

name: Cuttlefish
summary: A colour-changing cephalopod that hovers on a rippling fin skirt and shoots out two long tentacles to grab prey.
fact: Cuttlefish change colour and texture in fractions of a second using millions of pigment cells called chromatophores.

name: Bluespotted Ray
summary: A tan stingray covered in electric-blue spots that glides over sand hunting buried invertebrates.
fact: Stingrays crush shellfish with flat, plate-like teeth and defend themselves with a venomous tail barb.

name: Short-tail Electric Ray
summary: A round, plump ray that hides in sand and stuns prey with powerful electric discharges.
fact: Electric rays generate shocks with modified muscle tissue in two kidney-shaped organs beside the head.

name: White-spotted Guitarfish
summary: A shark-like ray with a flattened, wedge-shaped head that hunts crabs, squid and fish over sandy bottoms.
fact: Despite their shark-like tails, guitarfish are rays — their gills open on the underside of the body.

name: Whitemouth Moray Eel
summary: A speckled moray with a bright white mouth lining that hunts from dens at night, sliding through crevices.
fact: Morays have a second set of "pharyngeal" jaws that shoot forward from the throat to drag prey in.

name: Coral Grouper
summary: A brilliant red grouper sprinkled with blue spots that ambushes small fish from coral overhangs.
fact: Many groupers start life as females and later change into males.

name: Marbled Grouper
summary: A territorial, blotchy grouper that guards a cave or ledge and inhales anything edible that strays too close.
fact: Groupers feed by suction: opening their huge mouths creates a rush of water that pulls prey inside.

name: Lyretail Coral Trout
summary: A swift red grouper with a crescent-shaped, yellow-edged tail that chases fish in open water near the reef.
fact: The lyre-shaped tail is built for speed, unlike the rounded tails of most ambush groupers.
stylization: Listed as night-biased following the reference game; real lyretails also hunt by day.

name: Giant Grouper
summary: The largest bony fish on the reef: enormous, slow-turning, but able to inhale big prey in one gulp.
fact: Giant groupers can produce loud booming sounds with their swim bladders.
stylization: The booming sound is turned into a stylised "Sonic Boom" ability.

name: Football Trout
summary: A large, aggressive coral trout with bold black saddles that dominates the reef slope by day.
fact: Juveniles are thought to mimic a poisonous saddled pufferfish, gaining protection from predators.

name: Blacktip Reef Shark
summary: A sleek reef shark with ink-dipped fin tips that patrols shallow reef edges and hunts hardest at dawn and dusk.
fact: Blacktip reef sharks are often seen in water so shallow that their dorsal fins break the surface.

name: Great White Shark
summary: The ocean's most famous apex predator: a massive, torpedo-bodied shark with a broad diet of large prey.
fact: Great white sharks can sense tiny electric fields from prey with jelly-filled pores on the snout (ampullae of Lorenzini).
stylization: Great whites mostly live in cooler waters and only occasionally visit tropical reefs; the reference game included one as its final species.

name: Bluestreak Cleaner Wrasse
summary: A slender blue-and-black wrasse that runs a "cleaning station", picking parasites and dead tissue off visiting fish.
fact: Even large predators hold still with mouths open while cleaner wrasses work inside their gills.
stylization: Cleaning restores health quickly as a game mechanic; real cleaning removes parasites.

name: Banded Coral Shrimp
summary: A red-and-white banded shrimp that waves its long white antennae to advertise cleaning services at night.
fact: Banded coral shrimp usually live in pairs and defend their crevice from other shrimp.

name: Orange Coral Goby
summary: A tiny bright goby that perches between branching coral fingers and rarely strays far.
fact: Some coral gobies coat themselves in bitter, toxic mucus that deters predators.

name: Peach Fairy Basslet
summary: Peach-coloured basslets hover in glittering clouds above coral heads, picking plankton from the current.
fact: Anthias live in harems; if the dominant male dies, a female changes sex to replace him.

name: Dusky Anemonefish
summary: A dark orange anemonefish that never strays far from its host anemone, hiding among the stinging tentacles.
fact: A special mucus coating protects anemonefish from their host's stinging cells.

name: Gorgeous Prawn-goby
summary: A banded goby that shares a sand burrow with a nearly blind snapping shrimp, standing guard at the entrance.
fact: The shrimp keeps an antenna on the goby; when the goby flicks its tail in alarm, both dive into the burrow.

name: Yellow Seahorse
summary: A slow, upright fish that anchors its curled tail to seagrass and sucks tiny shrimp through its tube snout.
fact: In seahorses the male carries the eggs in a brood pouch and "gives birth" to the young.
stylization: Bony plates make seahorses a poor meal in the game — few predators bother with them.

name: Reef Crab
summary: A sideways-scuttling reef crab protected by a hard shell and pinching claws.
fact: Crabs regularly moult their shells to grow, and are especially vulnerable until the new shell hardens.

name: Common Reef Shrimp
summary: A small translucent shrimp that picks through rubble and seagrass and flicks backwards when startled.
fact: Shrimps escape predators with a rapid tail-flip that shoots them backwards.

name: Painted Lobster
summary: A colourful spiny lobster that hides deep in crevices by day with only its white antennae showing.
fact: Spiny lobsters lack big claws; they defend themselves with spines and by rasping their antennae to make sound.

name: Brittle Star
summary: A fast-crawling relative of starfish with five whip-thin arms that it can drop to escape a predator.
fact: Brittle stars regrow arms they lose to predators — so a bitten brittle star often survives.

name: Spiral Snail
summary: A slow grazing sea snail sealed inside a heavy spiral shell.
fact: Many reef snails graze algae films off rock and coral rubble, keeping surfaces clean.

name: Bristle Worm
summary: A segmented worm that wriggles out of sand and rubble to scavenge, then vanishes back underground.
fact: Polychaete worms are among the most abundant animals hidden in reef sediments.

name: Needle-spined Sea Urchin
summary: A black urchin bristling with long, brittle, mildly venomous spines. It grazes algae at night.
fact: Urchins keep algae from smothering corals; when urchins disappear, reefs can become overgrown.

name: Giant Clam
summary: The largest living clam, with a vividly coloured mantle that farms symbiotic algae in sunlight.
fact: Giant clams get much of their food from photosynthetic algae living in their mantle tissue.
stylization: The massive shell makes it inedible to every animal in the game.

name: Magnificent Anemone
summary: A large anemone carpeted with stinging tentacles — dangerous to most fish but home to anemonefish.
fact: Anemone tentacles fire microscopic harpoons called nematocysts to stun prey.

name: Blue Starfish
summary: A vivid blue sea star that glides over reef flats on hundreds of tiny tube feet.
fact: Sea stars can regenerate lost arms, and some can regrow an entire body from one arm.

name: Crown-of-thorns Starfish
summary: A many-armed starfish covered in venomous spines that eats living coral; outbreaks can devastate reefs.
fact: Humphead wrasse and the giant triton snail are among the few animals that eat adult crown-of-thorns.

name: Sea Cucumber
summary: A soft, sausage-shaped relative of starfish that vacuums sand for organic matter.
fact: Some sea cucumbers defend themselves by ejecting sticky, toxic threads.

name: Sea Slug (Nudibranch)
summary: A jewel-coloured sea slug whose bright colours warn: "I taste terrible".
fact: Many nudibranchs store toxic chemicals from the sponges they eat and use them for their own defence.

name: Barrel Sponge
summary: A tall sponge that filters thousands of litres of seawater through its body.
fact: Sponges are animals with no organs; water flows in through tiny pores and out through the top.

name: Bitter Sponge
summary: A bright red encrusting sponge loaded with defensive chemicals — only true sponge specialists can stomach it.
fact: Many sponges defend themselves chemically, since they cannot move or hide.

name: Plankton Swarm
summary: A drifting cloud of copepods, larvae and other tiny animals — shown as clusters of red dots.
fact: Zooplankton rise toward the surface at night in the largest daily migration on Earth.

name: Turf Algae
summary: A fuzzy carpet of fast-growing algae on dead coral and rock — the main food of grazing fish.
fact: Grazing fish keep algae trimmed, giving young corals space to settle and grow.

name: Seagrass
summary: Flowering marine plants that form meadows on sandy bottoms — nursery habitat for countless young fish.
fact: Seagrasses are true flowering plants, not seaweeds, and they store large amounts of carbon.

name: Coral Polyps
summary: Living coral tissue — thousands of tiny polyps that build the reef's limestone skeleton.
fact: Corals get most of their energy from symbiotic algae living in their tissues; losing them causes coral bleaching.

name: Sea Wasp (Box Jellyfish)
summary: A nearly transparent box jellyfish trailing long tentacles with one of the most potent venoms in the sea.
fact: Box jellyfish have 24 eyes and actively swim rather than simply drifting.
stylization: Rare hazard. In reality sea wasps mostly occur in coastal waters of northern Australia rather than on outer reefs.
